item.title: S&P/TSX composite up more than 100 points, U.S. stock markets mixed
item.description: Canada’s main stock index was up more than 100 points, helped by strength in the energy and base metal sectors, while U.S. stock markets were mixed.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index was up while markets in New York ended the week on a down note as a tech selloff deepened and oil prices climbed on Friday. The S&P/TSX composite index was up 39.45 points at 36,176.55. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 175.28 points at 52,002.41. The S&P 500 index was down 84.62 points at 7,659.44, while the Nasdaq composite was down 572.99 points at 26,140.03. The Canadian dollar traded for 70.65 cents US compared with 70.44 cents US on Thursday. The December crude oil contract was up US$2.52 at US$99.02 per barrel. The December gold contract was up US$11.00 at US$4,181.10 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026.

item.title: U.S. markets weighed down by extended sell-off in the tech sector
item.description: The S&P 500 was down 1.1 per cent as of 2:01 p.m. Eastern time and on track for a weekly loss. The benchmark index is pulling back from the all-time high it set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks closed lower on Wall Street as more drops for big tech companies weighed on the market. The S&P 500 lost 1.1 per cent Friday, and the Nasdaq composite sank 2.1 per cent. Both posted their worst week since June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average didn’t do as badly, and fell 0.3 per cent. Chip companies pulled back some more as worries deepened about how long the frenzy over the AI buildout will last. Micron Technology fell 5.6 per cent and Intel lost 5.8 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent. The price of Brent crude rose 3.7 per cent. THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below. Stocks fell on Wall Street Friday as another pullback in big technology companies weighed on the market. The S&P 500 was down 1.2 per cent as of 3:14 p.m. Eastern time and on track for a weekly loss. The benchmark index pulled further below the all-time high it set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 240 points, or 0.5 per cent. The Nasdaq composite was down 2.2 per cent and headed for its first weekly loss in five weeks. Weakness for AI stocks has been a major drag on the tech-heavy index this week. Declines in heavyweight tech stocks led the market lower. Micron Technology fell 4.9 per cent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 5.4 per cent, Broadcom was down 4.1 per cent and Intel lost 5.6 per cent. Among other tech companies in the red were Meta, which fell 4.4 per cent, and Google parent Alphabet, which gave up 2.9 per cent. It’s been a choppy week for chipmakers and other big tech stocks central to the artificial intelligence industry. Investors are now worried that the companies, which have relied on debt markets to finance an investment spree into their technology, may not be able to keep borrowing and spending as heavily with yields in bond markets worldwide recently climbing to their highest levels in years. Netflix’s stock fell 3 per cent a day after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about 6 per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Energy stocks held up better than most. Exxon rose 2.2 per cent and Chevron added 2.4 per cent. European and Asian markets closed higher. In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury slipped to 5.09 per cent from 5.10 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. Yields are down despite reports this week showing that inflation at the consumer and wholesale level rose more in the U.S. than economists expected. The reports could persuade the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate before the end of this year. The central bank increased its key interest rate by a quarter-point to about 3.9 per cent in September, its first increase in three years. Wall Street traders expect the Fed will keep its short-term rate unchanged at policy meeting this month, but the odds of a rate increase at the December meeting have jumped to 74.3 per cent from 50.2 per cent a month ago, according to data from the CME Group. On Friday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no fresh signals about potential interest rate policy moves by the Fed while attending a meeting of financial leaders in Bangkok. Elsewhere in the market, shares in Tesla fell 3.3 per cent after the electric vehicle company unveiled a new model of its Roadster sports car that can thrust itself up in the air. Alcoa rose 2 per cent and The Travelers Co. gained 1.6 per cent after the companies reported quarterly results that topped Wall Street forecasts. Expectations are high for growth in profits from all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and the many other worries weighing on Wall Street. In energy markets, oil prices remained elevated as the global oil supply continues to be under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.7 per cent to settle at US$109.86 per barrel. That is up from around US$72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July. The national average for gasoline is at US$4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the US$4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the US$3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary Friday. --- Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

item.title: European Investment Bank applies for exemption from foreign bank status
item.description: The European Investment Bank has applied for an exemption from foreign bank status in Canada, a move that would bring the lending arm of the European Union one step closer to operating here.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The European Investment Bank has applied for an exemption from foreign bank status in Canada, a move that would bring the lending arm of the European Union one step closer to operating here. The request was published today in the Canada Gazette, the government’s weekly publication listing new regulations and official notices. The bank and the Canadian government signed a letter of intent in March committing to look for new ways to work together in areas like critical minerals. The goal of that letter is to help ensure stable supply chains for various minerals and metals used in the clean energy, tech and defence sectors. The March letter says that while the arrangement does not create financial commitments, it was meant to start discussions on allowing the investment bank to operate in Canada. This application comes ahead of the Canada-EU Summit in Montreal at the end of October, where Canada and the EU are expected to announce the next steps in a deepening partnership. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026. David Baxter, The Canadian Press

item.title: U.S. fiscal 2026 budget deficit rises to US$1.99 trillion, largest in 5 years
item.description: The U.S. budget deficit rose by US$217 billion to $1.99 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, fuelled in part by tariff refunds and record spending to service the nation’s more-than $40 trillion in debt, ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: The U.S. budget deficit rose by US$217 billion to $1.99 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, fuelled in part by tariff refunds and record spending to service the nation’s more-than $40 trillion in debt, marking the largest budget shortfall in five years, Treasury Department figures reported on Friday showed. The results for the year ended September 30, the first full budget year of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term, compared to a $1.78 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025. It was the largest shortfall since fiscal 2021’s $2.77 trillion budget gap, then fueled by COVID-19 pandemic relief spending, and is the third- largest annual deficit ever. Total receipts for fiscal 2026 were a record $5.40 trillion, up $169 billion, or three per cent, from the $5.24 trillion in fiscal 2025. Fiscal 2026 outlays also were a record at $7.40 trillion, up $386 billion, or six per cent, from the $7.01 trillion in the prior fiscal year. Debt-service outlays totaled a record $1.36 trillion, climbing by $144 billion, or 12 per cent, a spending category now eclipsed only by Social Security and the combined outlays for Medicare and Medicaid. Total U.S. debt breached the $40 trillion milestone about two months ago. Another driver of the widening shortfall was a $22 billion drop in net tariff receipts following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year negating a large portion of the tariffs Trump had imposed during his first year in office. That triggered $145 billion of tariff refunds over this year, resulting in an 11 per cent decline in net tariff income to about $173 billion. A U.S. Treasury official said the department calculated an estimated deficit-to-GDP ratio of 6.2 per cent for fiscal 2026, but declined to say what GDP estimate was used. This figure compares to an actual 5.8 per cent deficit-to-GDP ratio for fiscal 2025. For the 2026 fiscal year’s final month of September, the Treasury reported a deficit of $27 billion versus a $198 billion surplus a year earlier. (Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci)
